item.title: [CBS News World] Zelenskyy says Ukraine hit 2 Russian ships off Libya, and 1 sank
item.description:
Kyiv, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country was behind an attack on a Russian warship off Libya on Sunday, claiming Ukrainian naval drones sank the vessel. It marked the latest attack in the North African nation tied to the Russia-Ukraine war.
Zelenskyy said Monday in a social media post that Ukrainian forces deployed seven domestically made naval drones in the operation, which sank a Russian corvette. The Ukrainian leader described the ship as one of Russia's newest vessels commissioned in 2023 during Russia's invasion.
"Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk," he wrote.
A satellite image shows a capsized Russian corvette and the northern area of the port after an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked at the Benghazi naval base, which Libya's eastern-based government said was caused by a suspected drone attack, in Benghazi, Libya, on Nov. 22, 2026. The vessel later sank, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Vantor / Handout via REUTERS
"We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons," he said.
Ukrainian forces also struck the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said Moscow used to transport weapons. He added that a Ka-27 military helicopter was destroyed in the attack.
Zelenskyy thanked the Security Service of Ukraine, known as the SBU, and other Ukrainian defense forces that took part in what he described as "an exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia's war."
Zelenskyy said he received detailed briefings on Sunday and Monday and that "the targets we set were achieved."
Russian officials made no immediate comment.

Indonesian rescuers race to find 34 missing workers after a deadly candy factory fire
Indonesian rescuers are searching for 34 missing workers after a deadly fire swept through a candy factory west of JakartaByNINIEK KARMINI Associated PressNovember 23, 2026, 1:26 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Indonesian rescuers searched Monday for 34 missing workers after a deadly fire swept through a candy factory west of Jakarta.
Saturday’s fire broke out at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia factory in Banten province. Firefighters battled flames for about 14 hours before largely containing the blaze tearing through the three-story building.
About 300 workers were inside the factory when the fire erupted, officials said. Of those, 63 were believed to have been in the hardest-hit area, mostly on the second floor where the flames originated from a cooling unit.
Indonesia’s National Search and Rescue Agency, or Basarnas, did not immediately offer a death toll, but said they collected human remains in 24 body bags for identification through forensic examination.
Meanwhile, rescuers saved 29 workers, five of whom were hospitalized, and continue to search for the missing.

item.title: [BBC World] Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
item.description:
Image source, Chris McGrath/Getty ImagesByJustin Rowlatt, Climate editor and Esme Stallard, Senior climate and science journalist, Reporting fromAntalya, TurkeyPublished3 hours ago
The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 bought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.
After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.
Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".
The world is preparing for life beyond 1.5C
This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.
The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.
Without agreement, that recognition has been lost.
Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:
Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding, external

item.title: [BBC World] Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Australia's Chris Bowen sits at the top table at the summit surrounded by other delegatesByJustin Rowlatt, Climate editor and Esme Stallard, Senior climate and science journalist, Reporting fromAntalya, TurkeyPublished22 November 2026Updated 5 hours ago
Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.
Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.
But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.
The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".
He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose country co-hosted the talks, attributed the failure to "difficult geopolitical times".
"That is the reality," he said on Monday.
After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday to try to break the deadlock.
But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023, when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.

item.title: [ABC News World] Okinawa celebrates restored Shuri Castle hall 7 years after fire
item.description:
Okinawa celebrates restored Shuri Castle hall 7 years after fire
Officials and residents in Okinawa have celebrated the restoration of Shuri Castle's main hall, marking a significant return of the island's cultural symbolByMARI YAMAGUCHI Associated PressNovember 22, 2026, 7:13 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
TOKYO -- Officials and residents in Okinawa celebrated the restoration of Shuri Castle's main hall on Sunday, its deep red exterior and dragon ornaments marking the return of a symbol of the island's heritage seven years after it was destroyed in a fire.
The fire on Oct. 31, 2019, destroyed several buildings at the castle complex in Naha, Okinawa’s prefectural capital, as it was hosting a festival. Firefighters struggled for nearly 12 hours to contain the blaze as it spread from building to building in strong winds. Investigators could not determine the cause but considered an electrical fault the likeliest explanation.
“The fire was a tremendous shock to the Okinawan people," Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja said at Sunday’s ceremony in the courtyard outside the main hall. "Seven years after the major loss, as we mark this milestone of the main hall restoration, I am deeply moved and delighted.”
The castle is a symbol of Okinawa’s cultural heritage dating to the Ryukyu Kingdom, which lasted about 450 years from 1429 until 1879, when Japan annexed the island.
It also represents Okinawa’s recovery from World War II. The castle burned down in 1945 during the Battle of Okinawa, which killed about 200,000 people, many of them civilians.
Koja thanked historians, artisans and other experts from across Japan who contributed to the restoration, as well as donors at home and abroad. He called for rebuilding the rest of the castle, saying the opening of the main hall, known as Seiden, is "not the end.”
The 2019 fire destroyed Seiden and two adjacent halls, as well as four nearby structures, while two other structures were heavily damaged.

Russian warship sinks in Benghazi after suspected Ukrainian drone attack
No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia
A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel.
The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government.
Initial reports said several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, triggering the explosion, the officials told the Associated Press.
View image in fullscreen
Aerial view of the Russian naval vessel Merkury before it was struck in the port of Benghazi, Libya, 21 November 2026. Photograph: 2026 Vantor/EPA
Satellite imagery showed the Merkury had sunk after the attack, which took place in the Mediterranean, more than 1,000 miles from south Ukraine, marking a notable geographic expansion of the now near five-year war.
Though Ukraine began the war with no navy, it has developed a sea drone capability that threatened Russian warships in the Black Sea. The Russian fleet has been forced to retreat to the eastern port of Novorossiysk because Sevastopol in occupied Crimea had become unsafe.

District court in the Hague finds Chinese carmaker infringed on intellectual property of Jaguar Land Rover
Chinese carmaker BYD has been banned from selling its “Defender clone” vehicle in the EU by a court in the Netherlands, after Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) brought a case saying it infringed intellectual property rights.
JLR launched legal action over the seven-seater Ti7 SUV earlier this year after BYD announced on its website that it was taking orders from UK customers for the vehicle. Earlier this month, bailiffs acting for JLR were reported to have seized digital records from BYD’s offices.
“In these summary proceedings, the preliminary relief judge rules that ​the Ti7 infringes the EU design of Jaguar Land Rover,” said the ruling from the district court in The Hague. “The characteristic ⁠and distinctive elements of the design are reflected in the BYD Ti7.”
View image in fullscreen
A Land Rover Defender 110 on display at the 2019 Frankfurt Motor Show in Germany. Photograph: Ralph Orlowski/Reuters
The ban will take effect one week after Friday’s ruling, which noted that BYD “currently has no concrete plans to place the Ti7 on the market in the EU”. The judge ruled, however, that the court had no jurisdiction over BYD’s activities in the UK.
BYD’s plug-in hybrid SUV, which has been on sale in China since last September, has been likened by motoring experts to the Land Rover Defender, with the BBC’s Top Gear magazine calling it the “Chinese Defender clone”.

Howard Lutnick, the beleaguered US commerce secretary and close ally of Donald Trump, is emerging as Democrats’ prime target when the party takes control of Congress in January.
Lutnick is resisting calls to resign amid a bipartisan outcry over his role in the scandal at artificial intelligence (AI) company Nvidia and the sale of microchips to China, the US’s principal geopolitical rival in the race for AI supremacy.
The 65-year-old billionaire received a vote of confidence from Trump on Friday but faces growing criticism from some Republicans and a chorus of Democrats vowing to investigate his actions and demanding that he testify on Capitol Hill. item.title: [ABC News World] In Ukraine, the fight to keep winter outside begins with a broken window
item.description:
In Ukraine, the fight to keep winter outside begins with a broken window
As the winter cold sets in, Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities face a growing shortage of window installers as Russian attacks leave homes shattered and families exposed to the coldByDMYTRO ZHYHINAS Associated Press and DEREK GATOPOULOS Associated PressNovember 22, 2026, 12:00 AM
KYIV, Ukraine -- For weeks after a missile exploded in front of her apartment block, Oleksandra Horban found pieces of glass in her small apartment.
She threw out her 2-year-old son’s plush toys which were covered with glass shards. Outside her ground-floor home, mangled window frames were piled onto a mountain of debris awaiting removal. Pieces of glass were mixed with autumn leaves on the muddy ground.
“Even now we still find glass,” Horban said. “If we vacuum three times, wash the floor and clean up, we’ll still find those microscopic pieces somewhere, in the bed or in the toys.”
As winter sets in, Ukraine is facing a severe shortage of replacement windows with Russian missile and drone attacks continuing to damage buildings, leaving residents exposed to the cold. Temperatures in Kyiv fell to minus 20 degrees Celsius (minus 4 degrees Fahrenheit) last winter.
Government assistance can take months, skilled installers are in short supply and replacement costs have soared, hitting low-income districts near industrial zones hardest.
Horban lives in a Soviet-era “groundscraper” - an enormous horizontal apartment block in the Ukrainian capital. A missile blast in October damaged a vertical section of apartments and shattered hundreds of facade windows.
Most shattered windows have been temporarily covered with fiberboard or tarps. Some boards have small openings fitted with Plexiglas to let daylight into apartments.
New windows in Horban’s apartment would cost about $1,700, more than three times the country’s average salary. Government compensation can take three to four months.

California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded
Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.
Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
The $75,000 reward offered by Chen Jie's family has sparked fears of more reckless climbing attemptsByKelly NgPublished20 November 2026
The Chinese embassy in Japan has warned its citizens against off-season ascents of Mount Fuji amid concerns that the hefty reward offered by a missing hiker's family could encourage more reckless climbing.
Chen Jie, 25, vanished on 8 November on the mountain. His family is offering 500,000 yuan ($75,000; £57,300) to anyone who finds him alive, and 100,000 yuan to anyone who recovers his body, say Chinese and Japanese media reports.
Strong winds and blizzards pose serious risks during the closed season, especially as shelter and first-aid centres are not operational, the embassy said on Tuesday.
Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from around early July to early September.
Earlier this year, authorities of Yamanashi province, where the northern part of Mount Fuji sits, had said that people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service from next year on.
Authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season to submit detailed climbing plans.
"We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Kotaro Nagasaki, the prefecture governor, said at the time.
On Wednesday, Nagasaki told reporters that attempts to find the missing climber could lead to "secondary disasters".
According to Japanese news outlet the Mainichi Shimbun, Nagasaki appeared to appeal to Chen's family, saying: "I understand that your family is important, but please refrain from doing anything that could endanger others."
Some social media users in Japan have similarly expressed fears would entice people to venture into the mountains ill-prepared and lead to more accidents.

The visuals of the historic trilateral meeting may be the only lasting impression left by the summitByAnthony ZurcherNorth America correspondentPublished19 November 2026
Donald Trump went into his trilateral meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping with little on the agenda and no clear asks – and he left with little in return.
In the end, the visuals of the meeting – the "optics", as political wags like to say – may be the only lasting impression from the summit, billed by some as a historic "Yalta 2.0" meeting of great powers.
The pomp and the ceremony, in the end, may be what the US president wanted most. item.description:

View image in fullscreen
Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, with one of the baobabs to be transported to Timbavati reserve in north-eastern South Africa. Photograph: Courtesy of Timbavati nature reserve
Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits
Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.
The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.
The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.
The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.
The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.
